articles.title: Rising medical costs are piling on for seniors already squeezed by inflation
articles.summary: Medical care expenses — one of the biggest costs seniors face — are rising, according to the latest Consumer Price Index data.
articles.body:
Medical expenses — one of the biggest costs seniors face — are rising fast with little relief in sight.

While overall consumer prices were up 0.4% month over month , according to the latest figures, older Americans have been slammed by rising healthcare costs for months.

Medical care items were up 0.5% and medical services rose 0.3%. Hospital services rose 0.8% over the month, and doctors' services increased 0.4%. Prescription drugs rose 0.3% in October.

Dental services, which are not covered by Medicare, jumped 0.8% in October and 0.5% the previous month.

The biggest jump was the cost of medical equipment and supplies, which rose 1.4% in October on top of 0.4% in September and 1.0% in August. This includes adhesive strips, heating pads, wheelchairs, a chair for the shower, and compression socks among other items regularly used by older Americans.

"What makes these rising healthcare costs so alarming is that they're affecting virtually every aspect of seniors' medical needs, from doctor and dental visits to prescription drugs, hospital stays, medical equipment, and home healthcare," Shannon Benton, executive director of the Senior Citizens League, a nonprofit advocacy organization, told Yahoo Finance.

The costs for nursing homes and adult care increased by 0.3% in October. Home healthcare rose by 0.2%.

"These aren't luxuries; they're necessities that older Americans often have little choice but to pay for. Seniors can't simply stop taking medications, skip necessary treatments, or go without nursing home or home healthcare because prices have gone up," she said.

"Seniors can't budget their way out of getting sick or needing medication."

Then there's the cumulative impact. Seniors are already struggling with higher housing costs, groceries, utilities, and Medicare premiums . "Now they're being asked to absorb even more increases in essential healthcare expenses, often on fixed incomes that simply aren't keeping pace," she said.

Roughly 15% of the average retiree's annual expenses will be health-related, according to Fidelity.

On average, a 65-year-old who leaves the workforce this year may need $185,500 in savings to cover out-of-pocket healthcare expenses throughout retirement even when enrolled in traditional Medicare. (Don't forget, Medicare isn't free , and it doesn't pay for everything.)

That estimate also doesn't include long-term care expenses, over-the-counter medications, and most dental services.

An apartment in an assisted-living facility is averaging $87,000 this year, according to the National Investment Center for Seniors Housing & Care — and costs go up as residents age and need more care. Units for dementia patients have an average rate of $105,000.

articles.title: Chip stocks' slide nears $5 trillion as Nvidia hits most extreme selling level since 2019
articles.summary: Nvidia and memory stocks are dragging chips lower again after a hot inflation report, even as most S&P 500 stocks hold up.
articles.body:
It took five minutes for Tuesday's hot inflation report to knock stocks lower, and chip stocks struggled to hold an early rebound. Nvidia ( NVDA ) hasn't been sold this hard, this fast since 2019, but the typical S&P 500 stock is barely down.

The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) was down nearly 1% midday Tuesday, shedding about $500 billion in market value according to Yahoo Finance calculations, while the PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) fell more than 1%. The equal-weighted S&P 500 ( ^SPXEW ), which gives every company the same weight, was down only about 0.2%.

Nvidia fell about 6%, slicing through the $170 level chart watchers flagged, and is on track for its lowest close since March 30 as the scandal surrounding CEO Jensen Huang drags on. Its relative strength index , a gauge of how fast and how hard a stock has moved, sank to 23 out of a possible 100 — its most oversold reading since June 2019.

Memory makers Micron ( MU ) and SanDisk ( SNDK ) and chip designer Arm ( ARM ) fell roughly 3% to 5%. AMD ( AMD ) and Broadcom ( AVGO ) held up after Monday's surge.

The longer view is starker. A Yahoo Finance basket of 62 chip stocks has lost about $5 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, roughly a quarter of its worth. That's more than the roughly $3 trillion the entire S&P 500 has shed over the same stretch, even though the basket includes some companies outside the index.

Tuesday's trigger was a hotter-than-expected October Consumer Price Index . S&P 500 futures fell about 0.5% in the five minutes after the 8:30 a.m. ET release, on volume many times the morning's norm. Nasdaq-100 futures briefly erased their losses by 10 a.m., then slid again.

Bonds felt it too. The 5-year Treasury yield ( ^FVX ) was on track for its biggest one-day jump since April 2025, and the 10-year ( ^TNX ) climbed back above 5% as traders raised bets on a December rate hike .

BofA's Savita Subramanian sees the bigger risk in the S&P 500 itself.

"We're not particularly bullish on the index. I think the index itself is a bit risky," the head of US equity and quantitative strategy at BofA Securities told Yahoo Finance on Tuesday. "What's the most crowded equity ticker in the world? It's the S&P index."

The typical stock looks nothing like the index. The equal-weighted S&P 500 is up about 4% since Oct. 6 and closed at a record on Nov. 4.

Some see Nvidia's slide as a chance to buy. "I think if [CEO Jensen Huang] stays, then this is going to prove to be overdone. And you know this will be a strong buying opportunity," Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon said Monday on Yahoo Finance's "Deirdre Bosa Live."

articles.title: Nvidia hires former acting U.S. attorney to probe Jensen Huang affair
articles.summary: Nvidia’s board of directors has hired a former prosecutor to probe events surrounding CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman believed to be a spy for China.
articles.body: Nvidia’s board of directors announced Tuesday that it has hired a prominent former prosecutor and a top Wall Street law firm to probe the events surrounding CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman believed to be a spy for China. “The independent members of the NVIDIA Board have retained former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a thorough and independent investigation as was announced on Sunday,” the company said in a statement. The announcement followed revelations over the weekend that included Huang’s admission that had an extramarital affair. The woman with whom Huang had the affair is widely believed to be Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and business executive. U.S. intelligence agencies believe that Huang spied for the Chinese government, sources told NBC News. As of Tuesday, Jensen Huang remained in his post as Nvidia’s CEO, and a spokesperson for the company told NBC News over the weekend that he was focused on leading the trillion-dollar AI chip giant “without interruption.” President Donald Trump said Monday that the Federal Bureau of Investigation was also probing the events. Trump said Huang “had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” adding, “I really believe him.” The recent developments have caused Nvidia shares to sell-off by more than 10% since trading opened on Monday morning. The move has erased almost $500 billion of value from the $4 trillion company in just two days. The sell-off was the latest blow in a weeks long decline for Nvidia stock already underway. After hitting its last record high on October 6, shares in the chip designer have plunged by 31%. That drop has erased more than $1.7 trillion in market value. Adding to the downward pressure on Nvidia shares Tuesday was new reporting from The New York Times that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had twice warned Trump about Huang’s entanglement with Chinese intelligence. “Trump was told aboard Air Force One in May en route to China that the United States had obtained sensitive intelligence showing that Nvidia’s chief executive was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy,” the Times reported. NBC News has not confirmed the report and has reached out to the State Department for comment. Rubio’s warning to Trump reportedly came shortly before Huang joined Trump aboard Air Force One during a pitstop in Alaska on its way to Beijing, where Trump was making a state visit. Huang had not been among the White House’s initial list of business leaders invited on the trip, according to reports at the time. But Trump denied this, writing on social media May 12 that Huang would be joining him on the state visit. “Jensen is currently on Air Force One,” Trump posted, mid-flight. On Monday, Trump was asked if he had been briefed about Huang before that trip. “I didn’t hear about it then,” Trump claimed. Pressed a second time about when he became aware of Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy, Trump said he would “have to check.” “They could have been mentioned,” he said. “Certainly, it didn’t make much of an impact on me.” “He’s an amazing guy,” Trump said of Huang, “I hope there’s no problem.” “If there is a problem, we’ll let you know about it,” the president continued, “but I hope there’s no problem.”
